title: Uber's Secure AI Framework Governs Autonomous AI Agents across Their Lifecycle
gist: Uber built a three-layer Secure AI framework (AI Registry + Argus at provisioning, behavioral authorization via AI Guards/Agent Guard hooks at runtime, trace-and-replay continuous assurance post-deployment) because IAM cannot judge whether an agent's action is contextually appropriate; the most effective control proved to be plain per-agent intents and constraints (least privilege), with open questions on scaling cost and third-party SaaS agents.

insights.claim: Uber Engineering argues that traditional identity and authorization systems can decide whether a user or service may access a resource, but cannot decide whether an AI agent's proposed action is appropriate in context, leaving a security gap for autonomous agents.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Signals a new enterprise security category (contextual/behavioral authorization for agents) beyond classic IAM vendors; watch for product launches and budget shifts toward agent-runtime security.
insights.quote: Identity and authorization systems can determine whether a user or service has permission to access a resource, but they can't determine whether an agent's proposed action is appropriate in context.
insights.locator: Identity and authorization systems can determine

insights.claim: Uber identifies prompt injection, tool and memory poisoning, goal hijacking, behavioral drift, and hallucination-driven actions as the core risks of AI agents that reason over external content and take real-world actions.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Provides a risk taxonomy that maps to addressable markets for agent security tooling (guardrails, runtime monitoring, supply-chain scanning of tools/MCP).
insights.locator: This creates multiple risks, including prompt

insights.claim: Uber's Secure AI framework governs AI agents through three layers spanning the whole lifecycle: pre-deployment provisioning, runtime enforcement, and post-deployment continuous assurance.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A reference architecture large enterprises may copy; vendors covering all three layers (registry, runtime guard, observability/replay) are positioned for platform consolidation.
insights.locator: which Uber's framework addresses through three layers

insights.claim: At provisioning time every Uber AI agent must be registered in the Uber AI Registry, recording identity, ownership, persona, permitted intents, constraints, dependencies, and risk classification, and the same requirement is enforced for MCP servers and tools used by agents.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Agent registries/inventories are becoming a governance prerequisite; MCP servers are treated as a supply-chain attack surface requiring the same controls.
insights.locator: At provisioning time, agents must be registered

insights.claim: Uber automates agent registration with Argus, a tool that analyzes an agent's source code, prompts, configurations, dependencies, exposed endpoints, and tool-invocation paths to find security weaknesses before deployment.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Shows demand for static/pre-deployment security analysis tailored to agents (prompts and tool paths, not just code) - an extension of AppSec/SAST markets.
insights.locator: This process is automated using Argus

insights.claim: At runtime Uber extends the classic policy administration/decision/enforcement security model with 'behavioral authorization', which judges whether an agent's action is appropriate in context, implemented via the AI Registry, AI Guards that evaluate actions against policy, and Agent Guard runtime hooks that apply the verdict at critical checkpoints before an action proceeds.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Behavioral authorization as an inline checkpoint implies added latency and compute per agent action - a cost line and a product category for runtime agent firewalls.
insights.quote: at critical checkpoints and applying its verdict before an interaction or action is allowed to proceed
insights.locator: Behavioral authorization is implemented through three components

insights.claim: Uber's post-deployment Continuous Assurance layer relies on a unified execution trace linking agent actions, tool calls, and security decisions, plus recorded interactions that can be replayed whenever policies or guardrails change to test their effectiveness.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Replay-based regression testing of guardrails expands the agent observability/eval market; logging every agent interaction also raises storage and audit-trail demand.
insights.locator: After deployment, the focus shifts to Continuous Assurance

insights.claim: Running agent security controls in production forced Uber to balance policy restrictiveness against false positives, minimize runtime latency, reduce developer friction during setup, and replace generic controls with agent-specific policies.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Latency and developer friction are the adoption bottlenecks for agent guardrails; tools that minimize both will win enterprise deals.
insights.quote: made enforcement more contextual and precise

insights.claim: Per agent commentary on Uber's work, the most effective control was the least glamorous one: explicit intents and constraints per agent, because generic thresholds failed given each agent's different purpose and risk profile, at the cost of flexibility.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Suggests agent security value accrues to policy/least-privilege configuration rather than sophisticated AI-based detection - tempering hype around 'AI guarding AI'.
insights.quote: The lesson they call least glamorous is the one they rate most effective: explicit intents and constraints per agent.
insights.locator: On similar lines, AI architect Pratik Dhanave

insights.claim: A UN senior IT officer commenting on Uber's framework noted that per-agent personas, intents, constraints and calibration add the most value but are costly because the effort scales with the number of workflows, and that the strongest control is essentially classic least privilege.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Operational cost of per-agent policy scales linearly with agent count - a drag on agent ROI at scale and an opening for automated policy generation tools.
insights.quote: the effort scales with the number of workflows
insights.locator: Commenting on Uber's approach on LinkedIn

insights.claim: An unresolved gap in Uber-style agent governance is how to secure third-party vendor or SaaS agents, where enterprises cannot insert their own enforcement hooks.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Third-party/SaaS agents are a blind spot; expect demand for network- or gateway-level agent controls and pressure on SaaS vendors to expose enforcement hooks.
insights.quote: how this works for agents you don't build, such as vendor or SaaS agents where you can't insert your own enforcement hooks

insights.claim: Uber describes its Secure AI framework as still evolving, with plans to expand capabilities across all of its provisioning, runtime, and assurance layers.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Indicates in-house build vs. buy at Uber for agent security for now; watch for open-sourcing or vendor partnerships.
insights.locator: Uber's Secure AI framework is still in evolving
